abstract.p: The present invention provides nucleic acids encoding the Doppel ("Dpl") protein, Dpl peptides, and assays utilizing the Dpl nucleic acids and/or peptides. In related aspects the invention features expression vectors and host cells comprising nucleic acids that encode a human Dpl polypeptide. The present invention also relates to antibodies that bind specifically to a human Dpl polypeptide, methods for producing human Dpl polypeptides, methods for identifying cells expressing Dpl, methods for using the Dpl gene and the Dpl polypeptide to alter cellular function and prion infectivity in culture or in vivo, and identification of individuals at risk for prion disorders by detecting alteration in Dpl coding and regulatory sequences and Dpl expression levels.

La présente invention concerne des acides nucléiques codant pour la protéine Doppel ("Dpl"), des peptides de Dpl, ainsi que des techniques utilisant les acides nucléiques et/ou les peptides de Dpl. Dans certains de ses aspects, l'invention concerne des vecteurs d'expression et des cellules hôtes contenant des acides nucléiques qui codent pour un polypeptide Dpl humain. L'invention concerne également des anticorps qui se lient spécifiquement à un polypeptide Dpl humain, des procédés de production de polypeptides Dpl humains, des procédés d'identification de cellules exprimant Dpl, des procédés d'utilisation du gène Dpl et du polypeptide Dpl pour modifier la fonction cellulaire et l'infectiosité du prion en culture ou in vivo, et l'identification d'individus risquant de développer des affections dues au prion par la détection d'une modification des séquences de codage et de régulation de Dpl et des taux d'expression de Dpl.

FIELD OF THE INVENTION This invention relates to nucleic acids, proteins encoded by such nucleic acids, and assays involving use of the these nucleic acids and/or proteins
BACKGROUND OF THE INVENTION

Pπons are infectious pathogens that cause central nervous system spongiform encephalopathies m humans and animals Pnons are distmct from bacteπa, viruses and viroids The predominant hypothesis at present is that no nucleic acid component is necessary for infectivity of prion protem Further, a pπon which infects one species of animal (e g , a human) will not readily infect another (e g , a mouse)

A major step in the study of pπons and the diseases that they cause was the discovery and puπfication of a protem designated pπon protem ("PrP") [Bolton et al , Science 218 1309-11 (1982), Prusmer et al , Biochemistry 21 6942-50 (1982), McKinley et al , CeU 35 57-62 (1983)] Complete pπon protem-encoding genes have smce been cloned, sequenced and expressed m transgenic animals PrPc is encoded by a smgle-copy host gene [Basler et al , Cell 46417-28 (1986)] and is normally found at the outer surface of neurons A leading hypothesis is that prion diseases result from conversion of PrPc mto a modified form called PrPSc

It appears that the scrapie isoform of the prion protem (PrPSc) is necessary for both the transmission and pathogenesis of the transmissible neurodegenerative diseases of animals and humans See Prusmer. S B . "Molecular biology of pπon disease," Science 252 1515-1522 (1991) The most common pπon diseases of animals are scrapie of sheep and goats and bovine spongiform encephalopathy (BSE) of cattle [Wilesmith, J and Wells, Microbiol Immunol 772 21-38 (1991)] Four pπon diseases of humans have been identified (1) kuru, (2) Creutzfeldt- Jakob Disease (CJD), (3) Gerstaann-Strassler-Sche nker Disease (GSS), and (4) fatal familial insomnia (FFI) [Gajdusek, D C , Science 197 943 -960 ( 1977), Medoπ et al , N Engl J Med 326444-449 ( 1992)] The presentation of human pπon diseases as sporadic, genetic and infectious illnesses initially posed a conundrum which has been explamed by the cellular genetic oπgm of PrP

Most CJD cases are sporadic, but about 10-15% are rnheπted as autosomal dominant disorders that are caused by mutations mthe human PrP gene [Hsiao et al , Neurology 40 1820-1827 (1990), Goldfarb et al , Science 258 806-808 (1992). Kitamoto et al , Proc R Soc Lond 343 391- 398 Iatrogemc CJD has been caused by human growth hormone deπved from cadaveric pituitanes as well as dura mater grafts [Brown et al , Lancet 340 24-27 (1992)] Despite numerous attempts to link CJD to an infectious source such as the consumption of scrapie infected sheep meat, none has been
identified to date [Harnes-Jones et al , J Neurol Neurosurg Psychiatry 51 1113-1119 (1988)] except in cases of latrogemcally mduced disease On the other hand, kuru, which for many decades devastated the Fore and neighboring tnbes of the New Gumea highlands, is believed to have been spread by infection dunng πtuahstic cannibalism [Alpers, M P , Slow Transmissible Diseases of the Nervous System. Vol 1, S B Prusmer and W J Hadlow. eds (New York Academic Press), pp 66- 90 (1979)]

The initial transmission of CJD to experimental primates has a nch history beginning with William Hadlow's recognition of the similaπty between kuru and scrapie In 1959, Hadlow suggested that extracts prepared from patients dymg of kuru be inoculated into nonhuman primates and that the animals be observed for disease that was predicted to occur after a prolonged mcubation peπod [Hadlow, W J , Lancet 2 289-290 (1959)] Seven years later, Gajdusek, Gibbs and Alpers demonstrated the transmissibihty of kuru to chimpanzees after incubation peπods ranging form 18 to 21 months [Gajdusek et al , Nature 209 794-796 (1966)] The similaπty of the neuropathology of kuru with that of CJD [Klatzo et al , Lab Invest 8 799-847 (1959)] prompted similar experiments with chimpanzees and transmissions of disease were reported in 1968 [Gibbs, Jr et al , Science 161 388-389 (1968)] Over the last 25 years, about 300 cases of CJD, kuru and GSS have been transmitted to a vaπety of apes and monkeys

The expense, scarcity and often perceived inhumanity of such experiments have restricted this work and thus limited the accumulation of knowledge While the most reliable transmission data has been said to emanate from studies usmg nonhuman primates, some cases of human prion disease have been transmitted to rodents but apparently with less regularity [Gibbs, Jr et al , Slow Transmissible Diseases of the Nervous System. Vol 2, S B Prusmer and W J Hadlow, eds (New York Academic Press), pp 87-110 (1979), Tateishi et al , Prion Diseases of Humans and Animals. Prusmer et al , eds (London Ellis Horwood), pp 129-134 (1992)] The importance of understanding the conversion of PrPc into PrPSc has been heightened by the possibility that bovine pπons have been transmitted to humans who developed vaπant Creutzfeldt- Jakob disease (vCJD), G Chazot, et al , Lancet 347 1181 (1996), R G Will, et al , Lancet 347921- 925 (1996) Earlier studies had shown that the N-terminus of PrPSc could be truncated without loss of scrapie infectivity, S B Prusmer. et al , Biochemistry 21 6942-6950 (1982), S B Prusmer, et al , Cell 38 127-134 (1984) and coπespondingly, the truncation of the N-terminus of PrPSc still allowed its conversion mto PrPbc M Rogers, et al , Proc Natl Acad Sci USA 90 3182-3186 ( 1993)

Recent studies have advanced the ability to visualize the structural transition of PrPc to PrPSo at a molecular level For example, the N-terminal portion is relatively unstructured and flexible, but assists m stabilizing structural elements withm the C-terminal portion D G Donne et al , Proc Natl Acad Sci USA 94 13452-13457 (1997) Furthermore, immunological studies have demonstrated that
N-terminal epitopes are cryptic in PrPSc, supporting the idea that this region undergoes profound conformational change dunng pπon propagation Peretz et al , J Mol Biol 273 614-622 (1997)

Despite these advances, the understanding of the structural biology of the pathogenic conversion process remams incomplete in many wa> s For example, it is unknown exactly which structural regions of PrPc are necessary or sufficient for conformational change to occur It is also unknown which regions of PrPSc are necessary or sufficient for infectivity Evidence mdicates that pnon stram phenomena and species barπers are encoded by alternative PrP conformations, but the precise structural determinants of these conformations have not yet been precisely identified Telling et al Science 274 2079-2082 (1996), Billeter, et al , Proc Natl Acad Sci USA 94 7281-7285 (1997) Recent studies have identified four residues of mouse PrP (MoPrP) that appear to mteract with protem X, a putative factor postulated to facilitate the conformational change from PrPc to PrPSc Telling, et al Cell 83 79-90 (1995) All four ammo acids come together to form the putative protem X bmding site in the tertiary structure of recombinant PrIP 90-231 and PrIP 29-23 I D G Donne et al , Proc Natl Acad Sci USA 94 13452-13457 (1997), T L James et al , Proc Natl Acad Sci USA 94 10086-10091 (1997) However, despite several reports of protems which bmd PrPc, the identity of protem X remams elusive Finally, although the structures of refolded, recombinant PrP molecules may resemble PrPc, a structural solution for PrPSc remams lacking

One strategy for determining PrP function is through the identification of protems similar to PrP, and the elucidation of the function of such protems The identification and study of pπon-related genes may offer insight into the general biology and progression of neurodegenerative disorders, as well as offering insight into the mechanistic alterations that result m pπon-mediated disorders There is thus a need m the art for the identification and study of genes encoding protems with similar structure and/or function

The terms "PrP gene" and "Prnp gene" are used interchangeably herein to describe genetic material which expresses proteins (for example those shown in Figures 3-5 of U.S. Patent 5,565,186 issued October 15, 1996) and polymorphisms and mutations such as those listed herein under the subheading "Pathogenic Mutations and Polymorphisms."
